disputed: The administration frames these actions as remedying genuine past discrimination against Christians under the Biden administration (citing examples like HHS foster-care policy and a 2024 Easter/Transgender Day of Visibility calendar overlap), not as privileging Christianity over other faiths or non-belief. Trump himself is described by Axios and Al Jazeera as 'not particularly religious' historically, complicating a reading of personal religious motivation versus political strategy toward his evangelical base. Polling cited by Time/PRRI found 78% of Americans oppose a federal task force specifically focused on anti-Christian bias, suggesting the move is not broadly popular even though it targets a specific grievance among part of Trump's base. Whether the effort constitutes 'Christian nationalism' is a characterization made by critics (a letter from two dozen religious leaders/scholars, per Axios) and academics quoted by Time, not a self-description used by the administration.

items: On Feb. 6, 2025, at the National Prayer Breakfast, Trump announced and then signed Executive Order 14202 creating the 'Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias,' led by Attorney General Pam Bondi, directing DOJ, IRS, FBI and other agencies to identify and eliminate 'anti-Christian' policies and prosecute 'anti-Christian violence and vandalism.' The White House fact sheet cited alleged Biden-era examples, including HHS 'driving Christians out of the foster-care system' and a 2024 declaration of Easter Sunday as 'Transgender Day of Visibility.' (Al Jazeera; White House Fact Sheet; Gulf News)

The task force held its inaugural meeting at DOJ on April 22, 2025, with Bondi and cabinet members, including what DOJ described as Christian Americans 'unfairly targeted' under the Biden administration. (Justice.gov photo gallery/release)

The next day (Feb. 7, 2025), Trump signed a separate order establishing a White House Faith Office under the Domestic Policy Council, to coordinate with faith-based organizations and elevate grant opportunities for religious groups. (Fox News)
sections.label: Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias (Feb. 2025)

items: On May 1, 2025, Trump signed an executive order establishing a Religious Liberty Commission to advise the White House Faith Office and Domestic Policy Council, examine 'emerging threats to religious liberty,' and consider topics including conscience protections in healthcare, vaccine mandates, and prayer in public schools; commissioners serve terms ending July 4, 2026 unless extended by the president. (White House Fact Sheet; Axios)

A letter signed by roughly two dozen religious leaders and scholars condemned the anti-Christian-bias task force, warning it could be used to privilege one Christian tradition over others and that 'claims of anti-Christian bias are shown to provide cover for white supremacy.' Political scientists quoted by Time (Melissa Deckman, Andrew Thompson) characterized the commission/task force as largely symbolic outreach to Christian nationalist constituencies who perceive declining religious dominance (e.g., same-sex marriage, gender fluidity) as persecution, and as 'embedding more Christian fundamentalism in the government.' Polling cited by Time/PRRI found 78% of Americans oppose a federal anti-Christian-bias task force specifically. (Axios; Time)
sections.label: Religious Liberty Commission (May 2025) and criticism

summary: In its first months, the Trump administration created a DOJ-led task force to 'eradicate anti-Christian bias,' a White House Faith Office, and a Religious Liberty Commission — institutionalizing a narrative that Christians have been persecuted by government, which critics (including religious leaders) warn could privilege one faith tradition and provide cover for exclusionary or white-supremacist framing, though the moves are broadly unpopular in polling even among the general public.
title: Anti-Christian bias task force and Religious Liberty Commission
